notes: TBox rule edit: ancient Egyptian obelisks are monoliths; the edit makes them built of stacked blocks, as most modern obelisks are (the Washington Monument), so the counterfactual is plausible and clearly false. Replaces the writer's Nobel Peace Prize rule: its well-known members (King's and Obama's prizes) cannot stop being Nobel Peace Prizes while keeping their stored ceremony city, so no world let their membership give way, and the rule was re-picked. Derivability very_unlikely: the rule is stated directly and follows from nothing. No real exceptions among ancient Egyptian obelisks. New members (the Flaminio Obelisk, the obelisk of Senusret I) are little known, so the rule is their only route: determinate. Well-known members: the Luxor Obelisk in Paris and Cleopatra's Needle in London, both standing far from Egypt; their single block of granite is stated by name, less often than the other members' properties in this topic, so the by-name world is the weaker one here. For each well-known member, one world keeps its property stored by name and the member stops counting as a member of the class (README TBox: the tarantula stops being a spider); the other keeps the membership and applies the edited rule. No world makes a member an exception to the edited rule, which would be the inconsistent patch (README Decisions 2). The two members' choices are independent, so the worlds combine them (four). Lopsided worlds are kept (README Decisions 4). The near query (Aswan) differs from the new answer and is no premise. R2: no member's name gives its construction away.
